title: No Single Best Leader
text:
In the 1950s and 1960s the psychologist Fred Fiedler studied leaders and their groups in many settings, from basketball teams and bomber crews to steel works, farm cooperatives and military units. He used an unusual questionnaire: each leader was asked to think of the person they had least liked working with and to describe that person. Leaders who still described their least preferred coworker in fairly positive terms were classified as relationship-oriented. Those who described them very harshly were seen as task-oriented.

Fiedler found that neither type was better everywhere. What mattered was the situation, which he described in three ways: how good relations were between the leader and the group, how clearly structured the task was, and how much formal authority the leader held.

When the situation was very favorable to the leader, or very unfavorable, task-oriented leaders tended to have the more effective groups. In the middle range, where things were mixed, relationship-oriented leaders tended to do better. Fiedler concluded that rather than trying to change their personalities, organizations should match leaders to situations, or change the situation to suit the leader.
lesson: A style that works in one setting can fail in another. Know your natural way of leading, and look for situations, or shape them, where it fits.
source: Fiedler, F. E. (1967). A Theory of Leadership Effectiveness. McGraw-Hill.
caveat: Later tests gave mixed support and the questionnaire was criticized, but the core idea that leadership effectiveness depends on the situation has endured.
